author: NorthEast News Desk
body: The Epsom Village Water District is operating with one commissioner and no clerk, secretary or treasurer, a staffing crisis that is delaying a planned PFAS treatment project and raising questions about the district’s future.

Commissioner Donna Dudley is the only remaining member of the board after a second commissioner resigned in August. The district serves about 320 connections and roughly 800 people, including Epsom Central School, the town hall, library, fire department and other public buildings. Its system also supplies water to local fire hydrants.

The vacancies make it difficult to assemble a quorum, approve engineering work and move the PFAS project to bidding. Residents are also confronting higher operating costs: the town’s annual hydrant rental charge rose from $9,000 to $40,000, according to the Concord Monitor.

A public meeting is scheduled for September 21 at 6 p.m. at Epsom Central School with town selectmen, state environmental officials and residents. One option under discussion is dissolving the village district and transferring the system to the town, a change that would require voter approval. Until governance is stabilized, the treatment project and other decisions remain constrained.
dek: A one-member board and vacant administrative posts are delaying bids for a treatment project while the district weighs whether the town should assume control.
headline: Epsom water district staffing crisis stalls PFAS remediation
